1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Piano
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5.background: One of the oldest recorded openings: Pedro Damiano recorded games in it at the beginning of the 16th century.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3.strategy: Defends e4 and prepares a slow, patient build-up: White avoids an immediate fight in the centre, keeps the tension, and plays for a manoeuvring game in which the centre is advanced only after careful preparation. The solid, modern way to play.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3.background: The name, Italian for "very quiet game", was given by Adolf Anderssen.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3.strategy: Prepares to build a broad pawn centre by taking control of d4, so that the d-pawn can advance and stay there. It is the classical approach: White wants the centre first and the initiative later, accepting that Black will challenge it at once.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3.background: Gioachino Greco consistently met 3...Bc5 with 4.c3, at a time when other players tended to play 4.O-O.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and defends e4, heading for a slow, symmetrical game. By delaying the central pawn moves White keeps its options open and sidesteps the sharper theory, but also gives up the quick grab of the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O.strategy: Gets the king safe first and decides on the central plan later: either the slow build-up with d3 or a central break at the right moment. Black gets a free choice of set-up in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4.strategy: Sacrifices a pawn to gain time: if Black takes, c3 comes with tempo on the bishop and d4 follows, building a big centre before Black is developed. White gets an initiative and open lines for the pawn; Black has to know the defence precisely.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4.background: Named after the Welsh sea captain William Davies Evans, the first player known to have played it, in a game against McDonnell in London in 1827. William Lewis published the first analysis in 1832, and the gambit became extremely popular.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d4.strategy: Strikes at once, offering a pawn for quick development: more of Black's pieces already bear on d4 than White's, so the pawn is usually lost, and White hopes for a quick attack on f7. The gambit is not quite sound, so White must play accurately.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d4.name: Italian Game: Rosentreter Gambit

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Bxf7+.strategy: Sacrifices a bishop, and soon a knight, for two pawns, hoping to expose the king for a mating attack. Black takes the pieces and defends, keeps a clear material advantage, and White has no real compensation.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Bxf7+.name: Italian Game: Jerome Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Bxf7+.background: Named after Alonzo Wheeler Jerome of Paxton, Illinois, whose game with it against William Shinkman was published in the Dubuque Chess Journal in 1876. It was a brief fad in the late nineteenth century but is almost never seen today.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4.strategy: Takes the pawn and accepts the challenge. Black is a pawn up, and White's compensation is time: the bishop on b4 is hit again after c3, so White builds a broad centre with tempo and a lead in development. Black's task is to find the moment to give the pawn back and defuse the attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6.strategy: Declines the pawn and keeps the bishop on its diagonal, so White cannot gain time with c3. But the move wastes a tempo, and White's b-pawn has gained space on the queenside, which gives White the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 d5.strategy: Strikes back in the centre at once, attacking both the bishop and the e4 pawn. After 5.exd5 the knight on c6 is attacked, but 5...Nxb4 saves it and removes the pawn that hits the bishop on c5. A sharp, offbeat reply that leaves White the choice.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 d5.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Hein Countergambit

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 b5.strategy: Hits the bishop with a pawn, but neither capture hurts White: after 5.Bxb5 Bxb4 the pawns are merely traded, and the bishop on b5 now attacks the knight that guards e5. Black has opened its own queenside and gets nothing in return.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 b5.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit, Fontaine Countergambit

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6.strategy: The natural reply: develops a piece, attacks e4 and prepares to castle. With the c-pawn on c3, White's b1-knight has no square to defend e4, so White must either defend it another way or strike in the centre at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7.strategy: Props up e5 with the queen so the centre holds, but it is a passive set-up: the queen may be misplaced on the e-file, and White can still take a full pawn centre and the space it controls.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and prepares to develop, but it is passive: White builds a broad pawn centre at once. Black's pieces are reasonably developed in return, and the position stays solid, if a little cramped.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it pressures e4, controls d5 and prepares castling. Black mirrors White's quiet set-up, so neither side commits the centre and the game is a patient fight over the right moment to open it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 f5.strategy: A gambit that tries to turn a quiet position into a sharp one: the pawn attacks e4, but it also weakens f7 and the diagonal to the king. White can take the pawn or simply develop, and Black has to prove its compensation, which is doubtful.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight with an attack on e4, which White's knight defends. The symmetrical structure leaves the centre unresolved and gives both sides a safe, flexible position from which to choose a plan.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.O-O Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, which nothing defends. White has to protect the pawn or give it up as a gambit, so Black takes the initiative while developing naturally.
